Q: Azure DevOps nuget restore fails with "Unable to find version 'x.x.x.x' of package" for internal feed package A:

The solution is to set the nuget version to 7.9.0.

Currently the actual version of nuget.

The solution in the YAML file looks like this:

- task: NuGetToolInstaller@1
    displayName: 'Use NuGet 7.9.0'
    inputs:
      versionSpec: 7.9.0
      checkLatest: true

Q: What is this Java function doing with the .dat file? A:

The main thing this method is doing is loading anims.dat as a binary resource and turning its contents into animation data.

getResourceAsStream("anims.dat") looks for the file on the classpath, then the BufferedInputStream is used to read the bytes. The loop appears to process up to 256 animation entries. For each entry it reads the animation name, speed, frame count, and then the frame data, storing the result in this.anim_list.

So this method isn't really interpreting the .dat file as a generic text/data file. It already assumes a specific binary layout for anims.dat and reads fields from that layout in a fixed order.

Without seeing the code that originally creates/writes anims.dat, though, it's hard to say exactly what each byte represents. The read... calls and the order they're used in are basically the file format definition here.

Q: How to make sure a user uploaded image is valid and safe before serving it to other users in rust? A:

I’d avoid trusting the uploaded MIME type or file extension on its own. A safer approach is to treat the upload as untrusted bytes, decode it with an image library, and validate the actual image format before doing anything with it.

I’d also put some limits around the decoder, such as maximum file size and maximum image dimensions. Otherwise a technically valid image can still be used to consume a lot of memory or CPU.

If the image only needs to be displayed to other users, re-encoding it into a known format can also be useful. That way you’re serving an image produced by your own decoder rather than the original uploaded file.

For the Rust side, I’d probably make the validation step explicit in the upload pipeline: size check → decode → validate dimensions/format → re-encode or store safely → serve with a fixed content type.

Q: Spark SparkOutOfMemoryError despite having each task memory greater than input A:

https://community.cloudera.com/t5/Support-Questions/spark-job-failure-with-no-space-left-on-device/td-p/197465.

This can be the issue.Spark keeps intermediate files in /tmp, where it likely ran out of space. You can either adjust spark.local.dir or set this at submission time, to a different directory with more space. Try the same job while adding in this during spark-submit; --conf "spark.local.dir=/directory/with/space"
